doc.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995

title: Recognition, his own band, and Lester Young drafted
summary: Tate is satisfied with his career; he tells how Lester was tricked by a policeman, drafted, and jailed in Alabama until Norman Granz got him out.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Now you talked about Lester saying he never felt that he never really made it big because I don’t think he would have said that because of any lack in the power of his playing because he knew he had imitators, he knew that a lot of people were trying to play like him. But once again here we are at an issue where the musician is not receiving the diagnostic thing back that he needs. Other musicians will come up to him and say, “oh man I love the way you play,” but he wasn’t getting the feedback that he needed in other arenas, you know? Do you feel that you’ve gotten some of the respect that you deserve, and if you could have gotten more what would it have been?

Well I don’t know. I don’t have too many, I don’t have too many gripes really. I’m kind of satisfied with the way I’ve done. Because see when I got my, after I got my, when I organized my band, I was the leader and I paid the salaries. You know for 21 years I was on the job, you know, one job. So I kind of made it up there. But Prez used to say, he would refer to people, they wasn’t no failure or anything but he acted like it. He referred, he says, “I don’t know,” he says, “all the ladies say they try to play like me, but they’re © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -8-

making all the money.” He says, “I’m not making any money.” So and he says, “sometimes I don’t know if they’re playing like me or I’m playing like them.” You know he said kind of things like that, you know? So he really didn’t make too much money because he was you know everybody was trying to stay out of the Army and a lot of musicians beat it because it was a lot of jobs and things then, you know with everybody going in, and the musicians just wasn’t Army material, you know. So I remember one time we were out in California, and this little guy came out there that night and had his chain and zoot suit, and chain, you know like Cab used to wear and all that kind of stuff. So he sit and partied with us all night, me and Sweets, I mean Harry Edison, and Lester. And after, we would take our break, we’d come over and he’d buy everybody drinks and everything. And Prez was drinking pretty heavy then. And so at the end of the night he pulled it back like this and showed he was a policeman. He says, “I want you to be at the induction center tomorrow morning at 9 o’clock. I know where you live.” And Prez had a heart attack almost, man. “Oh, my God” he says, “how could he be like that, I had confidence in the little guy, I started to give him a stick of pride.” I says, “you wouldn’t of been going through all of that,” cause he didn’t do to smoke pot, you know it started ringing too much. And you know he broke his heart, you know. So now they carried him down and sent him to Ft. Bragg, then they sent him to Alabama. And it was rough times in there. And he was down there trying to grow some marijuana patch and had him a little patch, and they put him in a brig and he told me he could only see through the hole about like that you know. And Norman Granz, you know the impresario, went down and got him out and he’s the one that got him out. So he was down in Alabama so Norm says, you know, was telling him who he was and everything. And he’s Jewish you know. They say, “well we don’t care no more about you than we do about him.” That’s what they told him. He says, “yeah but if you mess with me you hear about it.” So he got him out. But he went down after that.
